text:
**Short answer:** Pick a power station with at least 1,800 W of continuous AC output. Most single-burner induction cooktops draw up to 1,800 W, and the [Duxtop 9100MC class](https://powerstationmatch.com/devices/induction-cooktop) adjusts from 200 W to 1,800 W. Capacity (Wh) only decides how long you can cook.

**My pick: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 (~$899).** [Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/power-station-that-can-run-an-induction-cooktop) lists it as in stock with a 2,600 W inverter and 2,073.6 Wh. That gives you headroom to run a plate at full power, plus enough battery for several meals. [Buy it here](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-elite-200-v2). That page says the code DEALECTRIC saves $44.95 and is pre-applied by the link. Dealectric is also the seller, so treat its recommendation with that in mind.

**Why it works:**
- A 2,600 W inverter clears the 1,800 W cooktop load with room to spare. Stations rated exactly 1,800 W (the BLUETTI AC180 and EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus) [run a plate at its limit](https://dealectric.com/power-station-that-can-run-an-induction-cooktop).
- A 2 kWh unit gives roughly an hour of continuous cooking at a full 1,800 W after losses, according to [PowerStationMatch](https://powerstationmatch.com/devices/induction-cooktop). Real cooking uses much less. A 20-minute meal at mixed power levels typically uses 300–500 Wh.
- Boiling a litre takes about 90–110 Wh, so a 2 kWh unit is good for [roughly 16 boils or several meals](https://dealectric.com/power-station-that-can-run-an-induction-cooktop). That figure is simple arithmetic and ignores inverter losses of about 10%.

**Smaller or cheaper options:**
- [Homepowerfacts](https://homepowerfacts.com/can-it-run/induction-cooktop/) says the DJI Power 1000 is the smallest of the stations it tracks that can run a single-burner cooktop. But a 1,000 Wh unit only cooks for [about 45–50 minutes](https://www.blackoutwise.com/will-it-run/induction-cooktop) on high, since the burner cycles and averages about 1,080 W.
- The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 [stops at 1,500 W](https://www.blackoutwise.com/will-it-run/induction-cooktop). It will only work if you cook on a lower setting.

**What won't work:** Small stations in the 300–600 W class can't run a cooktop on high. That includes the EcoFlow RIVER 3 and RIVER 2 (about 300 W continuous), the RIVER 3 Plus and BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 (600 W), and the Jackery Explorer 300 v2 (300 W). Per [Blackoutwise](https://www.blackoutwise.com/will-it-run/induction-cooktop) and [Homepowerfacts](https://homepowerfacts.com/can-it-run/induction-cooktop/), they fall well short of the 1,800 W peak. The [Goal Zero Yeti 500](https://www.blackoutwise.com/will-it-run/induction-cooktop) (500 W) is also out.

**Electric kettle:** The results don't list kettle wattage, but I'd assume it's similar to the cooktop, since many kettles draw around 1,500 W. Check your kettle's label against your station's continuous output. A 1,800 W+ station that handles the cooktop should handle a kettle too.

**Tips to stretch the battery:**
- Bring food to temperature at full power, then drop to 400–800 W. [Cooking at level 5–6 instead of max can halve the battery used](https://powerstationmatch.com/devices/induction-cooktop).
- Cheap plates often hit low heat by [cycling 1,200 W on and off](https://dealectric.com/power-station-that-can-run-an-induction-cooktop), so size the inverter for those peaks.
- Give the station ventilation. Running near its limit makes it hot, and it may cut output to protect itself, [per VanLifeKitchens](https://vanlifekitchens.com/guides/can-a-power-station-run-an-induction-cooktop).

No station in the results can run a cooktop for a full day on one charge. For longer needs, plan to recharge with solar or the grid, or add an expansion battery.
